To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the RSV fusion protein is expressed in multiple forms in virus-infected Vero cell cultures, including an unglycosylated form, and that the F1 and F2 subunits are covalently linked to form the mature F protein.

the F1 and F2 subunits interact to form a stable trimeric F protein that is present on the surface of virus-infected cells, and that the F protein is glycosylated at multiple sites, with the F2 subunits displaying different glycosylation patterns.
the F2 subunits of RSV F protein can be glycosylated to different extents and that this results in multiple F protein species being expressed in infected cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the F2a/b subunit of the F protein of respiratory syncytial (RSV) virus.
the glycosylation and processing of the RSV fusion (F) glycoprotein and the effect of these processes on the structure, stability and biological activity of the protein.
the identification and characterization of the F protein of RSV and how it interacts with the F2 subunits.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the F protein is expressed as a single F1 monomer, a single F2 monomer and an F2 dimer, which is glycosylated in the latter form.
RSV F protein is expressed in multiple glycosylated species, which are expressed on the surface as equivalent F protein trimmers.
the RSV F protein is cleaved by a furin-like protease to produce F1 and F2 subunits, which interact to produce equivalent F trimers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
RSV F protein is expressed in multiple forms, including a 21 kDa F2a and a 16 kDa F2b, and that these are expressed on the cell surface as F1-[F2](a,b) trimers.
multiple glycosylated fusion proteins are expressed in RVS-infected cells and these are important in the fusion process.
the RSV F protein is expressed as a single F1 monomer and at least two forms of the F1 dimer, designated [F2](ab).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the RSV fusion protein is glycosylated in a complex manner and that the F2 subunits are not identical.
the F protein is expressed as two different glycoprotein forms, F1 and [F2](A/B), which interact to produce equivalent trimers on the surface of virus-infected cells.
multiple glycosylated species of F are expressed on the surface, and that the glycosylation of the F protein is important for the formation of the F trimers.
